name: Kurtöp
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source.
catalog_citation: Hyslop, Gwendolyn. 2011. A Grammar of Kurtöp. PhD dissertation, University of Oregon, Eugene. xxxix+729 pp. (open access, UO Scholars' Bank). Corroborated by Hyslop, Gwendolyn. 2021. Between Stress and Tone: Acoustic Evidence of Word Prominence in Kurtöp. Language Documentation & Conservation 15: 551-575 (open access, ScholarSpace, hdl 10125/74668).
catalog_quote: Kurtöp is another example of a tonal language that also has word-level stress and I argue that stressed syllables in Kurtöp can be identified by the following properties: 1) the obligatory presence of high or low tone; 2) the possibility of a complex onset or long vowel; and 3) the acoustic correlate of duration. ... In summary, the first syllable of words must bear a tone (either high or low). This obligatory presence of tone is a feature of Kurtöp stress. In addition to the obligatory presence of tone, stressed syllables are slightly longer. ... External evidence for first-syllable stress in Kurtöp comes from several sources. First is the intution I share with native speakers that first sysllables are somehow more prominent than other syllables. Second is the movement of tone to the leftmost edge of the word (i.e. the first syllable) when prefixed. ... [p. 204] The primary acoustic correlates of Kurtöp stress are duration and tone. ... [p. 226] In Kurtöp, phonological words can be identified by first syllable stress and the obligatory presence of tone. ... [Hyslop 2021: 557] Without exception, the initial syllable of the root is stressed. This will be the first syllable of the word, except in negated verbs, in which case stress is found on the second syllable. Negation is done by way of a prefix (the only prefix in the language; all other affixes are suffixes), but stress remains on the initial syllable of the verb stem.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kurtöp has lexical tone (H vs L, contrastive only after sonorant onsets, realized on the first syllable) plus word-level stress fixed on the first syllable of the phonological word; the stressed initial syllable obligatorily bears the H/L tone, alone licenses complex onsets and long vowels, and is longer (~10 ms) than the second syllable; intensity and vowel quality are not correlates.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described. Synchronically transparent noun compounds (e.g. phokhwi 'male dog') are said to have 'compound stress' as opposed to 'normal stress' (§11.3.2, p. 294), without further detail.
new_statements.exceptions: Footnote 79 (p. 247), added after the defense: in verbal negation stress appears to stay stem-initial and does not shift to the negative prefix má-, whereas tone does shift to the prefix — i.e. stress is stem-initial rather than strictly word-initial when a prefix is present (prefixes are otherwise rare). Bound suffixes/enclitics (e.g. -the) do not receive their own stress but are incorporated into the host word's stress pattern (p. ~310).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word (grammatical word plus optional particle/enclitics), §7.4 p. 226; evidence includes a production study of disyllabic words in a carrier frame (§7.2.1). Language is analysed as tonal-with-stress in Hyman's (2006) typology.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Kurtöp (ISO xkz, Glottolog kurt1248 'Kurtokha') as spoken in Dungkar geok, Lhuentse district, Bhutan; same languoid as the target. No dialect restriction relevant to the stress statement.

tone_statements.citation: Peralta, William. 2018. Tonogenesis: the perception of tone and the role of place of articulation in Kurtöp. Proceedings of the 6th International Symposium on Tonal Aspects of Languages (TAL 2018), Berlin, 83-87. ISCA.
tone_statements.quote: Kurtöp (Lhuntse dzongkhag, the Kingdom of Bhutan) is argued to be currently undergoing tonogenesis. Previous research has shown that this process had been completed in environments following the sonorants first, and subsequently following the palatal fricative [1]. These processes, however, are still being observed following the remaining obstruents. ... As the literature argues, the tonal contrast in Kurtöp first developed following sonorants, subsequently expanded to the palatal fricative, and is currently spreading to the dental fricatives and all stops.
tone_statements.summary: Emergent tone: contrast complete after sonorant/palatal-fricative onsets (credited to Hyslop 2009), incipient after stops per the author's own perception data; no tone inventory or labels given.

tone_statements.citation: Plane, Sarah. 2016. On the role of manner and place in Kurtöp tonogenesis. Long abstract, LabPhon15 (15th Conference on Laboratory Phonology, Cornell University, July 2016), abstract no. 120.
tone_statements.quote: This study builds on Hyslop (2009), showing that in the Tibeto-Burman language Kurtöp, place and manner of consonant trigger play a role in the development of tone. Hyslop (2009) has shown that in Kurtöp, tone first phonologized following sonorant consonants and then the palatal fricative and that tonogenesis is now underway following the remainder of the obstruents. ... Results also show that Kurtöp voiceless stops condition a fundamental frequency approximately 30 hertz higher than voiced stops, and that this difference is maintained over the duration of the vowel.
tone_statements.summary: Tone said to be phonologized only after sonorant onsets and the palatal fricative, still developing after other obstruents (F0 ~30 Hz higher after voiceless stops); no inventory or count given.

tone_statements.citation: Michailovsky, Boyd & Martine Mazaudon. 1994. Preliminary notes on the languages of the Bumthang group. In Per Kvaerne (ed.), Tibetan Studies: Proceedings of the 6th Seminar of the International Association for Tibetan Studies, Fagernes 1992, vol. 2, 545-557. Oslo: The Institute for Comparative Research in Human Culture.
tone_statements.quote: Tone register (high vs low): A high vs low contrast is found on words with nasal or continuant initials. Initial stops and sibilants also have distinctive tonal register, high for unvoiced (p, t, k, c, s, ɕ) and low for voiced (b, d, g, ɟ, z, ʑ). Voicing is often absent in pronunciation, leaving only the low tone to insure the contrast. Thus, ʑ- is usually pronounced ᴸɕ-. ... Typologically, the intersection of two tonal registers with a distinction between glottalized and smooth syllable types is typical of Tibetan dialects.
tone_statements.summary: Two registers, high/low: contrastive after nasal or continuant initials, tied to voicing on obstruents; open syllables also short smooth vs long glottalized. Own 1977-78 field data. No stress remarks.

sources.note: Kurtöp is undergoing tonogenesis; the study examines how sonority and place of articulation condition the spread of tone from onset voicing contrasts. Tone is more likely to be produced after fricatives than after stops, and within stops tone phonologises more readily after some places of articulation than others; tone is moving through the language from the most sonorous onsets to the least sonorous. Acoustic production study (56 pp.).

sources.note: Compiles a typology of tonogenesis from 40 languages across families, coding each tonogenetic event for syntagmatic position, manner and laryngeal setting of the trigger; distinguishes 'strict' tonogenesis (first acquisition of tone) from 'broad' (a tonal language adding tones); finds onset-conditioned tonogenesis prevalent and sonority important in strict tonogenesis, and argues the Vietnamese model does not fit most cases. Kurtöp is not named in the abstract; it is presumably one of the 40 languages (the author's own onset/sonority-conditioned case, and Hyslop & Plane 2024 'refine the model…
